title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
hookLine: God shrinks Gideon's army so no one will boast

lines: MINE OWN HAND HATH SAVED ME.
cards: Gideon finally has an army, and God's complaint is not that it's too small.

In the King James Bible: "The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." Too many.
Gideon's men camp by a spring, and below them in the valley lies the camp of Midian, "like grasshoppers for multitude," with camels past counting. Any sensible general would send for more troops.
Gideon is told to send people home.

teach.b: First cut: whoever is fearful and afraid may go home. The text says twenty-two thousand leave and ten thousand stay. Still too many.
Second cut: take them down to the water to drink. Some get down on their knees. Some lap, putting their hand to their mouth.
Three hundred lap, and those are the ones God keeps: "By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you."

teach.h: THE TEXT NEVER SAYS WHY THE LAPPERS.
teach.b: The text never says why the lappers. Some preachers say they were the alert ones, keeping their eyes up. Others say the test was arbitrary on purpose, and God simply took the smaller group.
Judges gives no reason for the test at all. The reason it does give is back in verse two: so Israel can't say, mine own hand hath saved me. Then the plan, and it's strange.
Each of the three hundred gets a trumpet and an empty pitcher with a lamp hidden inside.
In the night they spread out around the camp, blow the trumpets, smash the pitchers so the lights blaze out, and cry: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon."
And then: "they stood every man in his place round about the camp." They don't charge. They hold up their lights and stand still.
The camp panics and turns on itself.

teach.h: THE SWORD OF THE LORD, AND OF GIDEON.
teach.b: Notice the order of that cry: the LORD first, Gideon second. The chapter is built so that, afterward, nobody can tell it as a story about their own strength. Less isn't a punishment here.

teach.h: THEY STOOD EVERY MAN IN HIS PLACE.
teach.b: Less is how they find out who did the saving.

how: Some Christians tell the story of Gideon's three hundred to speak about God's strength showing up in human weakness, and some pair it with Paul's words in Second Corinthians that strength is made perfect in weakness.

games.q: you're Gideon. you've got ten thousand men left, and God says it's still too many. what's the test?
o: watch how they drink at the water.
games.why: three hundred lap the water, putting their hand to their mouth, and those are the ones kept. the text never says why.

practice: Name one thing in front of you that you feel under-equipped for: not enough time, money, help or sleep.
Instead of listing what you lack, count what you actually have, the way Gideon counted at the water: three hundred is a real number, and so is one free hour, two friends or forty dollars.
If you pray, bring the gap to God; if you don't, let the small number be enough for now.

wordCard.voice: Three hundred. The men who lapped the water: the army God made smaller, so no one could say, my own hand saved me.

orig.note: Hebrew: my own hand saved me, the boast God shrinks the army to prevent (Judges 7:2).
